solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Screens bank for weakness

blocks.note: window blinds screen a room from view
a pot is a bank of money, as in a kitty or jackpot

explanation.surface: Someone vetting a bank and finding it financially weak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screens' reads as a verb about checking, but it is a plural noun: window coverings. 'Bank' is the pool of money in a game.
explanation.definitionFit: An area where someone cannot see their own faults is a figurative vulnerability or failing.

clue.text: Coach full of sailors feels very hot

indicators.note: a vehicle full of passengers holds them inside it

blocks.note: a coach is a long-distance bus
the Royal Navy, abbreviated

explanation.surface: A sweltering coach crammed with sailors on a hot day.
explanation.walkthrough: RN, the Royal Navy, is the standard crossword abbreviation for sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin or a forehead that is extremely warm is said to be on fire, a common idiomatic usage.

clue.text: Sound off, given rum in outskirts of Ipswich

indicators.note: rum means odd or peculiar, so the letters end up in a strange order
placed in means set inside a surrounding pair of letters
the outskirts of a town are its edges, so only the outer letters count

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
first and last letters of the town's name

explanation.surface: Someone ranting after a few rums on the edge of Ipswich, a town in Suffolk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink but is the adjective for strange. 'Given' is not a link word here; it is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail or protest loudly against something is to speak out angrily, the colloquial sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Make uneasy male dons ready for a dance?

indicators.note: to don is to put on clothing, so the outer phrase wraps around the inserted letter

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for male
fit for a disco, i.e. prepared to go dancing

explanation.surface: A man unsettled by getting dressed up for a night out dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' suggests university fellows, but it is the verb meaning puts on. The question mark flags the invented phrase for being dance-ready.
explanation.definitionFit: To disconcert or embarrass someone is to unsettle them, a direct synonym of the verb phrase.

clue.text: Skills needed to raise issue

blocks.note: surface reading: the ability to bring a matter up at a meeting
setter's reading: issue means offspring, so this is the know-how of bringing up children

explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise issue' sounds like voicing a complaint, but issue is the legal word for children and raise means rear them.
explanation.definitionFit: The abilities and knowledge involved in bringing up babies and children well form a recognised body of practical expertise.

clue.text: Kick tenor missing note

indicators.note: something missing has been left out, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: the tenor of a speech is its general tone
N is the abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: A singer who fluffed a note gets booted out of the choir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tenor' looks like the singer, but it is the noun for general drift or mood. Removing N from that synonym leaves three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike a ball with the tip of the foot is a verb usage, as in poking it home.

clue.text: He may perhaps steal piano and flute

blocks.note: a crim is a criminal, someone who might steal
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly

explanation.surface: A thief making off with a piano and a flute from a music shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flute' tempts as the instrument alongside piano, but it is the verb for making ridges. Crim is informal Australian and British slang for criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: To press pastry or fabric into small regular folds or grooves is to make fluting, a crafting synonym.

clue.text: Commanding Officer carried over a drink

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
c/o is the bookkeeping abbreviation for carried over
taken as written

explanation.surface: A senior officer handed a drink across the mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carried over' looks like a reversal instruction, but it is the accounting term abbreviated c/o, giving the same two letters as the officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot chocolate beverage made from powdered cacao beans and milk is a familiar bedtime drink.

clue.text: Doctrine briefly troubles one member of Muslim sect

indicators.note: said briefly means cut short, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: an ism is any doctrine or ideology
ails means troubles, as in what ails you
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A single believer bothered by a theological doctrine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' sits after 'Doctrine' but trims the word that follows it, troubles, to three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ismailis are a branch of Shia Islam who follow the Aga Khan, so one follower belongs to that sect.

clue.text: Ordering lap dances, church folk start to tremble

indicators.note: letters that dance move about and swap positions
the start of a word is its opening letter only

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
Church of England, abbreviated
folk as people, men
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Churchgoers quaking at the sight of someone booking lap dances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordering lap dances' reads as a scandalous request; ordering is the definition, and lap is the fodder. CE stands for Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Arranging things in position or sequence is placement, as when seating guests at a dinner.

clue.text: One cramming viscount in possession of drugs into posh car

indicators.note: to be in possession of something is to hold it, so outer letters hold an inner group
going into something means being placed within its walls

blocks.note: a Rolls-Royce, abbreviated
Vis is an abbreviation for viscount
E is ecstasy, so two of them make drugs in the plural

explanation.surface: An aristocrat caught with narcotics being bundled into a Rolls.
explanation.walkthrough: Two nested insertions: the viscount goes between two ecstasy tablets, and that group goes between the two Rs of a Rolls-Royce.
explanation.definitionFit: A student swotting intensively before exams is studying hard, which British English calls revision.

clue.text: Eulogies once I am gone

indicators.note: gone in the sense of gone wrong or crazy, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone imagining the tributes that will be paid at their own funeral.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's 'once I am gone' is a stock phrase about death, which fits eulogies neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal expressions of high praise are tributes, the Latin plural of encomium being a learned synonym.

clue.text: Report of secretive life in Irish town

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: secretive is sly, and a go at life is a turn or innings

explanation.surface: Rumours about someone living a hidden life in a small Irish town.
explanation.walkthrough: Go here is the noun for a turn or attempt, as in having a go at life; sly plus go said together gives the place name.
explanation.definitionFit: This county town in the north-west of the Republic of Ireland is a well-known port.

clue.text: Bananas aren’t nice fruit

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so these letters run wild

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A fussy eater declaring that bananas taste nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the fruit in question; it is the anagram signal, and the fruit is the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A smooth-skinned variety of peach is a stone fruit, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: Protein in dairy item, for example

blocks.note: casein is the main protein in milk
taken as written
a pot of cream or yoghurt

explanation.surface: A note that casein is found in milk products, given as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' does double work as the two letters and as their position, sitting in the pot.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific instance illustrating a point being made serves as an illustration, the idiom's everyday meaning.

clue.text: Contemptuous expression of son leaving party

indicators.note: whatever is leaving departs, so that letter comes out

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
a bash is an informal party

explanation.surface: A parent's sneer as their boy storms out of a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: S is the genealogical abbreviation for son.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of scorn or dismissal, as Scrooge's humbug, is an interjection of disdain.

clue.text: Bishop and wife covering Greek festival, the latest fad

blocks.note: chess notation for bishop
taken as written
W is the abbreviation for wife
an agon was a public contest at an ancient Greek festival

explanation.surface: A cleric and his wife reporting on a fashionable Greek festival.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, covering means sitting on top, so the bishop-and-wife group comes above the festival rather than around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A popular trend that everyone hurries to join is jumped on, from the idiom about climbing aboard a parade cart.

clue.text: Intimate knowledge of face-lifts going wrong

indicators.note: something going wrong falls out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: Knowing the private details of cosmetic surgery that went badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' looks like a link word but belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The basic information about sex and reproduction, traditionally explained to children, is knowledge of intimacy.

clue.text: Duty gives way to enjoyment in special kind of railway

indicators.note: one thing giving way to another is replaced by it

blocks.note: your part is your role or duty
fun is enjoyment
particular means special

explanation.surface: A tourist line where obligation is set aside for pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the first four letters of the word for special with a three-letter word for enjoyment.
explanation.definitionFit: A cable-hauled mountain line with counterbalanced cars is a particular type of rail transport.

clue.text: Talks of people welcoming self-seeker, no saint

indicators.note: no means without, so those letters are dropped
to welcome someone is to take them in, so one word goes inside another

blocks.note: an egotist seeks only their own interest
standard abbreviation
a nation is a people

explanation.surface: A community admitting a selfish, far from saintly individual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talks' looks like a verb but is the plural noun; the singular answer is acceptable since talks and the answer are both a process of discussion.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal discussions aimed at reaching an agreement between parties are diplomatic bargaining.

clue.text: Explains away ultimately puzzling disappearances

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter counts

blocks.note: last letter of the word
things that go missing are losses

explanation.surface: An investigator dismissing some baffling vanishings.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb is followed by 'over' in common use, but on its own it still means to smooth over or play down.
explanation.definitionFit: To gloss something is to give a misleadingly favourable interpretation, covering up awkward facts.

clue.text: Characters facing embarrassment always tease and scoff

indicators.note: characters facing each word sit at its front, so take initial letters

blocks.note: first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: Someone constantly mocked and ridiculed for blushing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' looks like a partner to tease in the sense of jeer; it is British slang for devouring food.
explanation.definitionFit: In British informal usage to scoff is to wolf down food greedily, a slang synonym for consuming.

clue.text: Learned about boomerangs Buddhist men regularly used

indicators.note: a boomerang flies back, so this short word turns round
used at regular intervals means every other letter is taken

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A scholar who studied the boomerang habits of monks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Learned' looks like a past-tense verb, but it is the two-syllable adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Having or showing great scholarship marks someone as well-read and knowledgeable, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Shorn ewe followed by shaggy ram in agitated state

indicators.note: shearing strips the outside away, leaving only the core of the word
one piece coming after another sets them side by side in that order

blocks.note: middle letter once the outer letters are clipped
a shaggy coat is rough
tup is a dialect word for a ram

explanation.surface: A farmyard scene of a sheared ewe and a scruffy ram, both in a flap.
explanation.walkthrough: TUP is a British farming word for a ram, common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Being worked into a nervous or emotional frenzy describes someone highly worried or excited.

clue.text: Head of Logistics phoned up boss

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter
in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: first letter of the word
rang means phoned

explanation.surface: The logistics manager called the chief executive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' looks like the manager being phoned; it is the noun for a raised knob or stud, as on a tree trunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A knotty protuberance on wood or a tree is a raised swelling, the same sense as a decorative boss.

clue.text: Cold, shy, surly person

blocks.note: C for cold, as on a tap
to shy is to throw, as at a coconut shy

explanation.surface: A list of adjectives describing an aloof, grumpy character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' reads as timid in the list of traits, but it is the verb for throw.
explanation.definitionFit: An ill-mannered, boorish individual is rude and grumpy, from which the adjective churlish comes.

clue.text: Run on the level

blocks.note: first meaning: as two words, British slang for running away fast
second meaning: honest and above board

explanation.walkthrough: 'Run on the level' sounds like jogging on flat ground; the first sense is the slang phrase to leg it, meaning flee.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for legitimate, the word means honest and genuine, matching the idiom for straightforward dealing.

clue.text: Old playwright bitten by Greek bird

indicators.note: something bitten is held between the jaws, so it sits inside

blocks.note: abbreviation for Greek
O is the abbreviation for old
George Bernard Shaw, the Irish dramatist

explanation.surface: A veteran dramatist savaged by a Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw is the crossword's favourite playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: A large short-winged hawk used in falconry is a raptor, one kind of bird of prey.

clue.text: Guy slips clothes off

indicators.note: with the clothes off the outer covering is gone, so the edge letters drop

blocks.note: to skid is to slip

explanation.surface: A man stripping off his clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a noun for a man, but it is the verb meaning mock or tease.
explanation.definitionFit: To rib or tease someone playfully is to make fun of them, the British sense of guying.

clue.text: Near middle of pub, almost horizontal

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is cut

blocks.note: an inn is a pub
lying down is horizontal

explanation.surface: A drinker nearly flat out in the middle of the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle of pub' wants to give the central letter of pub; 'Near middle' is the definition, and the whole pub is shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: Situated inside or close to the centre is the dictionary sense of this rare adjective.

clue.text: Some concern as alarm sounded by hooter

indicators.note: some of means only part, so a run of letters sits within the words

blocks.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: A car horn sounded as a warning causes worry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooter' looks like a horn or siren, but it is British slang for the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Sounds produced through the nose are described with this adjective, as with a nasal twang.

clue.text: Cleaner of busy royal fellow

blocks.note: a busy is British slang for a police detective, abbreviated det
Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher
a gent is a man or fellow

explanation.surface: The cleaning lady of a hard-working royal man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busy' looks like an adjective but is old British slang for a police officer or detective.
explanation.definitionFit: A soap-like chemical used for washing dishes or clothes is a cleaning agent.
